phase1.intro:
Think about how a workshop organizes its own blueprints once there are more than a couple lying around — packages are exactly that filing system for Java classes.

Where should we start?

topics.buttonText: How do I declare and name a package?
dialogue: A `package` declaration [[key:must be the very first line in a file]] (before even imports), and the convention is a reversed domain name — `com.mycompany.util` — specifically so two different companies' folders can never accidentally collide under the same name.

stickyNote.flavor: 📁 first line in the file, reversed-domain naming
stickyNote.definition: package com.mycompany.util; must be the file's first line. Reversed domain naming avoids collisions between different organizations' packages.

topics.buttonText: How do I actually use a class from another package?
dialogue: Once a class lives in a package, anything that wants to borrow it needs an `import` — `import com.mycompany.util.MathUtils;` pulls in exactly that one blueprint, while `import com.mycompany.util.*;` pulls the whole folder in at once.

[[key:There's exactly one folder Java hands you automatically, no request needed]]: `java.lang`, which is why `String`, `System`, and `Math` all just work without any import at all. Everything else needs an explicit import, or a [[term:fully qualified name]] instead.

stickyNote.flavor: 📥 java.lang is the one free folder
stickyNote.definition: import pulls in a class or whole package (with *). java.lang is auto-imported (String, System, Math); everything else needs an explicit import.

topics.buttonText: Why bother organizing code into packages at all?
dialogue: [[key:Why bother organizing code this way at all]]? Mainly to avoid naming collisions — two unrelated libraries can both have a class called `Vector` and never conflict, as long as they live in different folders — plus it keeps related blueprints grouped logically.

stickyNote.definition: Packages prevent naming collisions between unrelated classes with the same name, and group related classes together logically.

phase1.openingDialogue: Packages are the filing system for Java classes — a naming convention, an import system, and a way to dodge naming collisions. 🗂️

phase2.errorMessage:
Main.java:5: error: cannot find symbol
        ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
        ^
  symbol:   class ArrayList
  location: class Main
Main.java:5: error: cannot find symbol
        ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
                                      ^
  symbol:   class ArrayList
  location: class Main
2 errors
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:ArrayList lives in java.util, and java.util is NOT automatically imported]] — only `java.lang` gets that free pass. Without an explicit import, the compiler has genuinely never heard of `ArrayList`.

[[key:The fix is one line at the top of the file]]: `import java.util.ArrayList;`. Or, if you'd rather skip the import, you can always use the fully qualified name directly: `java.util.ArrayList<String> list = new java.util.ArrayList<>();` — more to type, but it works without any import at all.

mcq.question:
Which package is the ONLY one automatically imported into every Java file?

A) java.util
B) java.io
C) java.lang
D) java.time

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create a package structure:
• com.example.shapes
• In it, create Rectangle and Circle classes with area() methods
• In a Main class (can be in same file), import and use both shapes

Note: For simplicity, we'll put everything in one file with package declarations.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: the reverse-domain-name convention for packages (com.mycompany.util) isn't just a popular habit — it's an official recommendation baked right into Oracle's Java Language Specification, specifically so that as long as everyone owns their own domain name, two companies' package names can never accidentally collide.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you organize more code~
